name: PowerView - Find Interesting ACLs
description: Searches the domain for non-default, potentially abusable ACL entries. Returns objects where controlled principals have GenericAll, GenericWrite, WriteOwner, WriteDACL, AllExtendedRights, ForceChangePassword, or AddMember rights over other AD objects. These entries are the entry points for ACL-based privilege escalation chains.
source: CPTS Module 13: Active Directory Enumeration & Attacks
notes:
=== WHY ACL ENUMERATION MATTERS ===
AD permissions are stored in Discretionary Access Control Lists (DACLs) on every
object. Admins often misconfigure these during delegation tasks, when adding
service accounts, or migrating permissions. The result: low-privilege users end
up with powerful rights over high-privilege accounts or groups.

BloodHound can show these visually, but PowerView gives raw access for targeted checks.

=== KEY RIGHTS TO LOOK FOR ===
  GenericAll       → full control over the object (can do everything below)
  GenericWrite     → modify non-protected attributes (set fake SPN for kerberoasting;
                     set scriptPath/logonScript for code execution)
  WriteOwner       → change the object's owner (take ownership = GenericAll)
  WriteDACL        → modify the object's ACL (grant yourself or others any right)
  ForceChangePassword (AllExtendedRights) → reset the object's password without knowing it
  AddSelf/AddMember → add members to a group
  AllExtendedRights → all extended rights including ForceChangePassword, DCSync rights

=== CRITICAL CHAIN EXAMPLE (Module 13 Lab) ===
wley → ForceChangePassword → damundsen
  wley has ForceChangePassword over damundsen. Reset damundsen's password.
damundsen → GenericWrite → Help Desk Level 1 (group)
  damundsen can add anyone to Help Desk Level 1 group. Add yourself.
Help Desk Level 1 → AddSelf → IT Admins (group)
  Members of Help Desk Level 1 can add themselves to IT Admins. Do it.
aclbuster (IT Admins member) → WriteDACL → Domain object
  Can modify domain object's DACL. Grant yourself DCSync rights.
DCSync everything.

=== OUTPUT COLUMNS ===
  ObjectDN       → target object (what you're gaining rights over)
  ActiveDirectoryRights → the right (GenericAll, WriteProperty, etc.)
  SecurityIdentifier → who has the right (SID of the holder)
  IdentityReferenceName → human-readable name of the rights holder

=== BLOODHOUND IS OFTEN BETTER ===
Find-InterestingDomainAcl can produce massive output and takes time.
BloodHound's pre-built query 'Find Principals with DCSync Rights' and
'Shortest Paths to Domain Admin' are faster for overall picture.
Use Find-InterestingDomainAcl for targeted verification and lab exercise paths. Also covered in: OSCP PEN-200 Chapter 21 (Active Directory Introduction and Enumeration).

defense.why_it_works: Find-InterestingDomainAcl (PowerView) / BloodHound enumerates ACEs to find objects where the current principal has abusable rights (GenericAll/Write, WriteDACL, ForceChangePassword, AddMember).
defense.prerequisites: Valid domain credentials and LDAP access.
defense.impact: A list of ACL-based privilege-escalation paths (who can act on what).
defense.detection: [MITRE T1222.001] LDAP enumeration of object ACLs (4662; Defender for Identity recon); BloodHound collection.
defense.prevention: Audit ACLs regularly (ADACLScanner/BloodHound) and remove non-standard ACEs; detection-focused since reads are built-in; enable Directory Service Access auditing.
defense.evasion: A single scoped ACL read blends with normal LDAP; BloodHound stealth mode reduces the fan-out.
defense.misconfiguration: Non-privileged users or groups have been granted sensitive AD object permissions (WriteDACL, GenericAll, GenericWrite, ForceChangePassword, AddMember, etc.) through misconfigured delegation, 'inherited from parent' ACEs copied at provisioning time, or direct one-off grants. Because AD ACEs are not surfaced in the normal GUI, these often persist for years.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# Example: a help-desk group has ForceChangePassword on Domain Admins members
# Found via BloodHound 'ForceChangePassword' edge, or PowerView:
Get-ObjectAcl -Identity 'Domain Admins' -ResolveGUIDs |
  Where-Object {$_.ActiveDirectoryRights -match 'ResetPassword'} |
  Select-Object IdentityReference, ActiveDirectoryRights, ObjectType

# Another dangerous pattern — GenericWrite on a user (enables targeted Kerberoasting):
Get-ObjectAcl -Identity 'svc_sql' -ResolveGUIDs |
  Where-Object {$_.ActiveDirectoryRights -match 'GenericWrite'}
defense.secure_config:
# 1. Run AD ACL audit quarterly (automated):
# BloodHound: Mark all Domain Admins as 'High Value', find paths from low-priv users
# PowerView batch:
Get-DomainObjectAcl -ResolveGUIDs |
  Where-Object {$_.ActiveDirectoryRights -match 'GenericAll|GenericWrite|WriteDACL|WriteOwner'} |
  Where-Object {$_.IdentityReference -notmatch 'Domain Admins|Enterprise Admins|SYSTEM'} |
  Export-Csv acl_review.csv

# 2. Remove dangerous ACEs:
Remove-DomainObjectAcl -TargetIdentity 'svc_sql' \
    -PrincipalIdentity 'helpdesk' -Rights GenericWrite

# 3. Enable AD Protected Users group for privileged accounts
# 4. Use tiered administration (Admin Tier 0/1/2) to limit blast radius
